# Motivation

## Why this talk {.smaller}

- NAS (2009) and PCAST (2016): scientific validity of firearms examination has not been established
- @cuellar2024methodological: literature search of 28 black-box validation studies
  - Found six flaws (A–F) present, with minor exceptions, in **every** study
  - Concluded: none of the existing studies can establish scientific validity
- @chin2026towards responded: a flaw in one study doesn't doom the whole evidence base
  - Draws on evidence-based medicine / systematic-review practice
  - Argues for a **cumulative** forensic science: openness, registration, meta-analysis

::: {.notes}
~1 min. Set up the stakes: these error-rate studies are cited in criminal trials.
Don't relitigate all 28 studies — just enough to motivate the disagreement.
:::

## The six flaws {.smaller}

| Flaw | Description | Cuellar et al. framing |
|---|---|---|
| A | Inadequate sample size | Exacerbates the other flaws |
| B | Non-representative sample (examiners, firearms, ammunition) | Damages the data |
| C | Non-representative testing conditions (contextual bias, known-test effects) | Damages the data |
| D | Inconclusives treated as correct or ignored | Fixable if raw responses available |
| E | Invalid or nonexistent uncertainty measures | Fixable if raw responses available |
| F | Missing data handled inappropriately | Fixable if missingness can be characterized |

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This table *is* the paper's Table 1 — don't read it verbatim,
point at rows B and D/E specifically since those anchor the two case studies.
:::

## Where we agree with Chin et al.

- Not every flaw has the same consequences
- Analytic shortcomings (D, E) may be **repairable after the fact** — if the raw
  responses were recorded
- Imperfect studies can still inform the design of *future* studies
- We should not discourage data collection just because a study can't stand alone

::: {.notes}
~1 min. This concession slide matters rhetorically — it shows the talk isn't
just restating the 2024 paper, it's sharpening it in response to real pushback.
:::

## Where we push back

> "The problem is not simply that the wrong quantity was reported... The
> problem is that the data needed to estimate the relevant quantity were
> never collected in the first place." — response to @chin2026towards

- Some flaws (B, C) operate on **study design and sampling**, not analysis
- No amount of reanalysis recovers information that was never observed
- **Claim of this talk:** the six flaws split into two qualitatively different
  buckets — remediable (fixable via reanalysis) and non-remediable (fixable
  only with new data)

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This is the thesis statement — say it out loud, slowly. Everything
after this slide is in service of defending this one claim.
:::

# The Remediable / Non-Remediable Distinction

## What "remediable" means here

Fix a target quantity (the **estimand**):

> the population-average examiner error rate (FPR / FNR), under casework-representative
> firearms, ammunition, examiners, and testing conditions

- **Remediable**: given the raw examiner-by-item responses, the estimand can
  still be validly estimated (possibly with extra assumptions / new analysis)
- **Non-remediable**: the sampled data cannot support the estimand, *regardless*
  of what analysis is applied to them

::: {.notes}
~1 min. Naming the estimand explicitly is what makes the rest of the flowchart
legible — don't skip this slide even though it feels abstract.
:::

## Flowchart: sorting the six flaws

<!-- TODO: replace with a designed figure (e.g., built in the design skill or
     as a standalone SVG/graphviz diagram). Placeholder logic below. -->

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Flaw] --> B{Operates on data<br/>collection or analysis?}
    B -->|Analysis / reporting| C{Raw responses<br/>available?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Remediable<br/>— recompute]
    D1["D: inconclusive handling"] --> D
    D2["E: uncertainty measures"] --> D
    B -->|Collection / design| E{Population distribution +<br/>covariates captured?}
    E -->|No, in practice| F[Non-remediable<br/>without new data]
    F1["B: non-representative sample"] --> F
    F2["C: non-representative conditions"] --> F
    B -->|Sample size| G[Remediable<br/>by pooling / more data]
    G1["A: inadequate sample size"] --> G
    E -->|Yes, with assumptions| H[Gray zone:<br/>remediable w/ sensitivity analysis]
    H1["F: missing data"] --> H
```

::: {.notes}
~2.5 min. This is the centerpiece slide — go slowly. Walk the tree left to
right: A is variance-only (more data fixes it); D/E are pure reanalysis;
F needs an assumption but is at least partially recoverable; B/C are the
hard cases because the studies never characterized the population they'd
need to correct for.
:::

## Reading the tree

- **A (sample size)** — noise, not bias. More examiners / comparisons fixes it.
- **D, E (inconclusives, uncertainty)** — pure reanalysis of existing responses.
- **F (missing data)** — recoverable only under a stated missingness assumption;
  the honest "gray zone."
- **B, C (sample, conditions)** — the estimate is biased for a population that
  was never characterized. Reweighting would require information the studies
  don't have.

::: {.notes}
~0.5–1 min transition slide into "now let's show this, not just assert it."
:::

# Data-Generating Process

## Why simulate?

- The 28 studies can't be un-run — we can't observe the "true" error rate they missed
- A simulation with a **known ground truth** lets us show, precisely, what each
  flaw does to a study's conclusions
- Same generative model powers both case studies — only the lever we pull differs

::: {.notes}
~0.5 min.
:::

## Notation {.smaller}

Complete crossed design: every examiner evaluates every item.

- Items $i = 1, \dots, I$; examiners $j = 1, \dots, J$; $n = IJ$ total responses
- $\operatorname{expit}(x) = 1/(1+e^{-x})$, the inverse logit link
- Baseline rates (hyperparameters): $p_{FP}, p_{FN}, p_{IC} \in (0,1)$
- Heterogeneity (hyperparameters): $\sigma_Q$ (item difficulty), $\sigma_S$
  (examiner skill), $\sigma_T$ (examiner inconclusive tendency)

::: {.notes}
~0.5 min. Just orient the audience to the indices before the equations land.
:::

## Item and examiner models {.smaller}

$$
G_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(\rho), \qquad
d_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0, \sigma_Q^2), \qquad i = 1,\dots,I
$$

$$
s_j \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0, \sigma_S^2), \qquad
\tau_j \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0, \sigma_T^2), \qquad j = 1,\dots,J
$$

with $G_i, d_i, s_j, \tau_j$ mutually independent across $i,j$.

**Decision challenge** for pair $(i,j)$:
$$
c_{ij} = d_i - s_j
$$

Harder item ($d_i$ large) or weaker examiner ($s_j$ small) $\Rightarrow$ larger $c_{ij}$.

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. $G_i$ = ground truth (1 = same-source). $\rho$ = match_rate.
:::

## Response probabilities {.smaller}

$$
\pi^{err}_{ij} = \operatorname{expit}\Big[\operatorname{logit}(p_{FN})\,\mathbb{1}\{G_i=1\} + \operatorname{logit}(p_{FP})\,\mathbb{1}\{G_i=0\} + c_{ij}\Big]
$$

$$
\pi^{inc}_{ij} = \operatorname{expit}\Big[\operatorname{logit}(p_{IC}) + 0.5\,c_{ij} + \tau_j\Big]
$$

If $\pi^{err}_{ij} + \pi^{inc}_{ij} \ge 0.95$, rescale both by
$\kappa_{ij} = 0.95 / (\pi^{err}_{ij}+\pi^{inc}_{ij})$ so response
probabilities stay valid.

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. The 0.5 weight on $c_{ij}$ in the inconclusive term and the 0.95
cap are both ad hoc constants in the current code — flag as a limitation if
asked, and put a sensitivity analysis on the to-do list.
:::

## The response, formally {.smaller}

Let $e(G) = $ "elimination" if $G=1$, "identification" if $G=0$ (the *error* label),
and $c(G) = $ "identification" if $G=1$, "elimination" if $G=0$ (the *correct* label).

$$
R_{ij} \mid G_i, c_{ij}, \tau_j \;\sim\; \text{Categorical}
\begin{cases}
e(G_i) & \text{w.p. } \pi^{err}_{ij} \\
\text{"inconclusive"} & \text{w.p. } \pi^{inc}_{ij} \\
c(G_i) & \text{w.p. } 1 - \pi^{err}_{ij} - \pi^{inc}_{ij}
\end{cases}
$$

independently across $(i,j)$ given the latent variables above.

<!-- TODO: add a firearm-level random effect (firearms nested within

     sampling), but would be needed if CI coverage (Flaw E) is added later as
     a second remediable-flaw example. See backup slide "Appendix: firearm
     clustering" for the planned extension. -->

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This slide is the payoff of the notation build-up — say the plain-
English version too: "an error, an inconclusive, or a correct call, with
probabilities that shift based on how hard the item is and how skilled the
examiner is." Don't let the audience get lost in the categorical notation.
:::

## Calibrating to real studies

- Baseline rates and heterogeneity currently loosely set; next step is
  anchoring to published summary statistics, e.g.:
  - Ames II: proportion of "hard" cartridge-case comparisons per individual
    Beretta pistol ranges **0%–62%** across otherwise-identical firearms
    [@cuellar2024methodological]
  - Scurich et al. (2025): inconclusive rate 39.3% (blind) vs. 56.4%
    (known test) at the Houston Forensic Science Center
- Goal: every number on later slides should be traceable to either the
  simulation or a cited empirical estimate — not an arbitrary constant

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This slide doubles as a credibility signal — show the audience
you're not hand-waving the parameters.
:::

## One dataset, two designs

- **Case study 1** perturbs the *analysis* of a properly-sampled dataset
  (adds firearm-level clustering; compares CI methods)
- **Case study 2** perturbs the *sampling* itself (draws a non-representative
  subset of firearm types / examiners from the same population)
- Same DGP, same code base — the only thing that changes is which flaw is
  "switched on"

::: {.notes}
~1 min. Bridge slide into the two case studies.
:::

# Case Study 1: A Remediable Flaw

## Setup: inconclusive handling (Flaw D)

- Black-box studies handle inconclusive responses inconsistently — excluded,
  folded into "correct," or otherwise treated as if they don't affect the
  error rate
- @cuellar2024methodological recommend a bounding procedure instead: recode
  every inconclusive as an identification, then as an elimination, and
  report **both** recomputed error rates as a range
- Sharper point from working through the algebra: for how Monson, Smith, and
  Bajic (2023a) define these rates, the number a study **reports** already
  equals one of the two bounds — it is not a neutral middle ground
- Claim: this is *remediable* — both numbers come from the same raw
  responses, recomputed after the fact

::: {.notes}
~1 min. The "reported = one of the bounds" point is the hook — it means the
commonly-cited error rate was never a best estimate, it was already the
optimistic end of a range nobody reported the other end of.
:::

## Simulation design

- Same DGP as the rest of the talk, at the retuned defaults, under the
  study's actual incomplete design (50 examiners, 30 of 300 items each)
- For each simulated study, compute both numbers from the same raw
  responses:
  - **Reported**: identifications / all different-source cases (and the
    same-source analog for the false negative rate)
  - **Worst case**: recode every inconclusive as the error-favoring label,
    recompute
- Repeat across 100 replicate studies to check the gap is a stable pattern,
  not a fluke of one random draw

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min.
:::

## Results

- One example study: FPR **1.3% → 42.1%**, FNR **3.0% → 38.9%** — same raw
  responses, same study, wildly different numbers depending on a reporting
  choice made after data collection
- Across 100 replicate studies (means): FPR **1.6% → 38.7%**, FNR
  **3.3% → 40.4%** — the gap holds up, it's not one unlucky draw
- [FIGURE: boxplots of reported vs. worst-case FPR/FNR across 100 studies,
  faceted by rate — see icfis/case_study_inconclusive.qmd]

::: {.notes}
~2 min. Lead with the one-study numbers (concrete, easy to say out loud),
then the 100-study means as the "this isn't a fluke" follow-up. The boxplot
figure should show both distributions barely overlapping.
:::

## Why this counts as remediable

- The fix required **no new data collection** — the same raw examiner-by-item
  responses already support both numbers; only how they're summarized
  changed
- This is exactly the kind of flaw Chin et al. are right about: a study with
  this flaw alone can still contribute to a cumulative evidence base, *once
  reanalyzed*
- Contrast with what's next: no reanalysis of these same responses can fix a
  non-representative sample

::: {.notes}
~0.5 min. Land the point before moving to the harder case.
:::

# Case Study 2: A Non-Remediable Flaw

## Setup: non-representative sampling (Flaw B)

- Precondition for validity: firearms, ammunition, and examiners must
  represent the **full spectrum of real casework** [@cuellar2024methodological]
- None of the 28 studies demonstrate this
- Chin et al.'s response: non-representative samples can still contribute to
  a cumulative literature if combined with other studies / moderator analysis

::: {.notes}
~1 min.
:::

## Simulation design: three beats

1. **Biased estimate.** Draw a convenience sample of firearm types (e.g.,
   oversampling easier-to-classify makes/models) from a heterogeneous
   population; show the naive error-rate estimate is biased for the
   population-average estimand.
2. **The fix that could work.** *If* the population distribution of firearm
   types and their difficulty were known, and each study recorded firearm
   make/model, post-stratification / reweighting would recover an unbiased
   estimate — this is Chin et al.'s "moderator" / big-team-science suggestion.
3. **The fix that doesn't exist.** The actual studies neither characterize
   the target population of firearms in casework nor consistently record the
   covariates needed to reweight. The correction in (2) is not available in
   practice.

::: {.notes}
~2 min. This is the slide to get right — beat 2 is what keeps this honest
(we're not claiming reweighting is impossible in principle), beat 3 is what
makes it non-remediable *for the existing studies*.
:::

## Results [placeholder]

- [FIGURE: naive estimate vs. true population FPR, across degrees of
  sampling bias]
- [FIGURE: same comparison, with and without the (unavailable) reweighting
  correction]
- Expected story: bias grows with the degree of non-representativeness;
  reweighting closes the gap only when population + covariate information
  exists, which it doesn't for any of the 28 studies

::: {.notes}
~2 min.
:::

## Why this counts as non-remediable

- No statistical procedure applied to *this* dataset can recover the
  population-average estimand
- Fixing it requires **new data** collected under a design that characterizes
  the target population — not a different analysis of the same responses
- This is the sharpest version of the paper's disagreement with Chin et al.

::: {.notes}
~1 min.
:::

# Conclusion

## Takeaways

- Not all six flaws are alike — sorting them by *remediable vs. non-remediable*
  clarifies exactly where Chin et al.'s cumulative-science argument applies
- **Remediable** (A, D, E, and F with assumptions): reanalysis of existing
  data can recover a valid estimate — Chin et al. are right here
- **Non-remediable** (B, C): the target quantity was never within reach of
  the sampled data — no reanalysis fixes this

::: {.notes}
~1 min.
:::

## Recommendations

- Report raw, examiner-by-item responses (not just summary error rates) —
  enables post-hoc correction of remediable flaws
- Pre-register sampling frames and characterize the target population of
  firearms / examiners *before* data collection
- Use cluster-aware / MRMC statistical methods designed for the dependence
  structure of validation studies
- Distinguish, explicitly, between flaws a study can outgrow and flaws that
  require a new study

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min.
:::

## Appendix: contextual-bias extension (Flaw C) {.smaller}

Hawthorne shift, calibrated to Scurich et al. (2025) blind vs. known-test
inconclusive rates at the Houston Forensic Science Center:

$$
\delta_H = \operatorname{logit}(0.564) - \operatorname{logit}(0.393)
$$

Under the "known test" condition, the inconclusive-probability equation
gains one term (error probability is unaffected):

$$
\pi^{inc}_{ij}(\text{condition}) = \operatorname{expit}\Big[\operatorname{logit}(p_{IC}) + 0.5\,c_{ij} + \tau_j + \delta_H \cdot \mathbb{1}\{\text{condition} = \text{"known test"}\}\Big]
$$

::: {.notes}
Backup only. Use if asked why the FPR/FNR barely moved between conditions
in the case-study-2 exploratory run — the shift is currently uniform across
easy and hard items, which is exactly why it doesn't move conclusive-only
error rates much. That's a modeling choice worth revisiting, not a result.
:::

## Appendix: missingness extension (Flaw F) {.smaller}

$$
\text{is\_error}_{ij} = \mathbb{1}\{R_{ij} = e(G_i)\}
$$

$$
\pi^{miss}_{ij} = \operatorname{expit}\Big[\operatorname{logit}(0.05) + 0.8\,c_{ij} + 1.2\cdot\text{is\_error}_{ij} + 0.6\cdot\mathbb{1}\{R_{ij}=\text{"inconclusive"}\}\Big]
$$

$$
M_{ij} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi^{miss}_{ij}), \qquad
R^{obs}_{ij} = \begin{cases} R_{ij} & M_{ij} = 0 \\ \texttt{NA} & M_{ij} = 1 \end{cases}
$$

A missing-not-at-random mechanism: harder pairs, errors, and inconclusives
are all more likely to drop out, which is what biases naive (listwise-
deletion) error rates downward.

::: {.notes}
Backup only.
:::

## Appendix: planned firearm-clustering extension {.smaller}

Needed only if CI coverage (Flaw E) is added as a second remediable-flaw
example. Not needed for either case study as currently built (inconclusive
handling and non-representative sampling). Not yet implemented.

- Introduce firearms $k = 1, \dots, K$, each with a latent firearm effect
  $f_k \sim N(0, \sigma_F^2)$ (e.g., make/model differences in how easy they
  are to classify — cf. the 0%–62% "hard" range across individual Beretta
  pistols in Ames II)
- Items are nested within firearms rather than exchangeable: $d_i \to d_{i(k)} = f_k + d_i$
- Responses for items sharing a firearm are then **dependent** given $f_k$,
  which is exactly the structure a naive Clopper–Pearson interval ignores
  and a cluster-robust / MRMC interval accounts for

::: {.notes}
Backup only — this is the concrete build item to report progress on if
asked "what's left to do."
:::
